### Problem: Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array {#sec-gcd-p1-arrgcd}

::: {.p-statement}
**Greatest common divisor of the smallest and largest.** Given an integer array
`nums`, return *the greatest common divisor of the smallest and the largest element of
the array.* The gcd of two numbers is the largest positive integer that divides both.

For `nums = [2, 5, 6, 9, 10]` the smallest element is $2$ and the largest is $10$, and
$\gcd(2, 10) = 2$: no integer larger than $2$ divides both endpoints.

**Constraints.** $2 \le n \le 1000$; $1 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 1000$.
Source: [LC 1979 · Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
This problem is a two-line trick wearing a number-theory costume. The answer depends on
only two of the $n$ elements - the smallest and the largest - so the entire array is a
distraction from a scan for two values followed by one call to Euclid. The thing worth
studying here is not the gcd but *how few passes* you need: the definition reads the
array twice (@sec-gcd-a2's folding idea in miniature), and one streaming pass can carry
both running endpoints at once.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Fold the min, fold the max, Euclid them.** Take the statement literally: two
   linear passes, then `gcd`. The reference every later rung is checked against.
2. **One streaming pass.** Track `(lo, hi)` together and gcd them once at the end -
   same answer, half the reads, and the shape you need when the array is a stream.
:::

::: {#fig-gcd-p1-arrgcd}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["index", "0", "1", "2", "3", "4"],
                   ["value", "2", "5", "6", "9", "10"]],
           colors={(1, 1): "blue", (1, 5): "green"}, cell_w=1.35)
V.show(draw)
```

Only the two shaded cells matter: the smallest value (blue, $2$) and the largest (green,
$10$). $\gcd(2, 10) = 2$ is the answer; the three interior elements never enter it.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Two passes - fold the min, fold the max

::: {.form-next}
One pass folds out the smallest element, a second folds out the largest, and `math.gcd`
finishes it. Two passes, each $O(n)$, plus one Euclid on numbers at most $1000$ wide.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("arrgcd", "scan")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def ag_scan(nums):
    mn = min(nums); mx = max(nums)
    return math.gcd(mn, mx)

assert ag_scan([2, 5, 6, 9, 10]) == 2
assert ag_scan([7, 7, 7]) == 7
assert ag_scan([1, 1000]) == 1
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long mygcd(long long a, long long b) {
    while (b) { long long t = a % b; a = b; b = t; }
    return a;
}

int agScan(vector<int>& nums) {
    int mn = *min_element(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    int mx = *max_element(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    return (int) mygcd(mn, mx);
}
```

:::

#### One pass - stream the endpoints, gcd at the end

::: {.form-next}
The two reads are unnecessary. A single scan keeps a running `(lo, hi)` pair and gcds
them once the loop ends. Same answer $\gcd(2,10)=2$, half the traffic, and the pattern
that generalises to a stream you can only pass over once.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("arrgcd", "fold")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def ag_fold(nums):
    lo = hi = nums[0]
    for v in nums:
        lo = min(lo, v); hi = max(hi, v)
    return math.gcd(lo, hi)

assert ag_fold([2, 5, 6, 9, 10]) == 2
for _ in range(200):
    a = [random.randint(1, 1000) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 20))]
    assert ag_fold(a) == ag_scan(a)
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long mygcd(long long a, long long b) {
    while (b) { long long t = a % b; a = b; b = t; }
    return a;
}

int agFold(vector<int>& nums) {
    int lo = nums[0], hi = nums[0];
    for (int v : nums) { lo = min(lo, v); hi = max(hi, v); }
    return (int) mygcd(lo, hi);
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time.** $O(n + \log V)$ for either rung - a linear scan to find the two endpoints plus
one Euclid on numbers at most $V = 1000$ wide. **Space.** $O(1)$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **All elements equal.** `nums = [7, 7, 7]`: min and max are both $7$, so the answer is
  $7$, not $1$. Never special-case it.
- **A 1 present.** If the smallest value is $1$, then $\gcd(1, \text{anything}) = 1$ and
  the answer collapses to $1$ no matter how large the maximum is.
- **Streaming seed.** The one-pass fold seeds `lo = hi = nums[0]`; seeding `0` instead
  pins the minimum to $0$ and returns the wrong gcd.

**Debug tip.** If the answer is $1$ for an array whose endpoints clearly share a factor,
you folded the gcd of *every* element somewhere instead of just the two endpoints - the
whole-array gcd and $\gcd(\min, \max)$ are different quantities.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Confusing $\gcd(\text{whole array})$ with $\gcd(\min, \max)$. Here a common divisor of
  everything must divide the smallest element, so the fold happens to agree only because
  the answer is defined on the endpoints - do not carry that coincidence elsewhere.
- Running Euclid on the array *indices* rather than their *values*.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-gcd-p1-strgcd turns the same $\gcd$ into a *string* period;
@sec-gcd-p2-split reuses the running-gcd fold as a greedy cut, and @sec-gcd-p3-subseq
folds the gcd of *sets* rather than single values.
